A yashmak is a type of face veil traditionally worn by some Muslim women, most closely associated with Ottoman Turkey and certain parts of the broader Islamic world.

A yashmak is not a single piece of cloth. It is made up of two separate pieces of thin fabric — usually white or a light color — worn together on the face:

  • One piece covers the upper part of the face: from the forehead down to just above or at the bridge of the nose.
  • The other piece covers the lower part of the face: from just below the eyes, covering the nose, mouth, and chin.

When both pieces are in place, they overlap slightly in the middle, and the result is that only the eyes are left uncovered. Everything else — forehead, nose, cheeks, mouth, chin — is hidden behind the fabric.

The yashmak is rooted in the Islamic tradition of modesty (known more broadly as purdah or hijab — the general principle of modest covering for women in public). In cultures where this tradition was practiced strictly, women would cover not just their hair and body, but also their face when going out. The yashmak was the specific garment used to fulfill that face-covering requirement.

It was especially common during the Ottoman Empire era, where it was a standard part of a respectable woman's appearance in public.
How it differs from similar veils

This is important, because there are several kinds of face and head coverings in Islamic tradition, and they are not the same thing:

  • Hijab — covers the hair, ears, and neck, but leaves the face fully visible. Very widely worn today.
  • Niqab — a face veil that covers everything except the eyes, usually made of a single piece of fabric. Similar in effect to the yashmak, but typically one piece, not two.
  • Burqa — covers the entire body from head to toe, including the face, but with a mesh screen over the eye area so the woman can see out while remaining entirely hidden.
  • Yashmak — specifically a two-piece arrangement covering the face, leaving only the eyes exposed. Its defining feature is this double-cloth construction.

So the yashmak sits somewhere close to the niqab in terms of how much it covers, but it is a distinct garment with its own traditional form.
What it looks like in practice

Imagine a woman standing in a busy marketplace. She is wearing a long robe and a headscarf. But when you look at her face, you see only her eyes — the rest of her face is covered by two layers of thin, pale fabric that meet across the bridge of the nose. That is the yashmak. The fabric is usually fine and lightweight, not thick or heavy, so it is not suffocating to wear.

The yashmak, in its traditional Ottoman form, is largely historical today. It was most common in the 19th and early 20th centuries and declined as the Ottoman Empire gave way to modern Turkey, which moved toward more Westernized dress codes. However, the broader idea of face-covering veils continues in various forms (like the niqab) across different parts of the Muslim world.

You might encounter the word "yashmak" today primarily in:

  • Historical writing about the Ottoman period
  • Literature from the 19th or early 20th century
  • Dictionary or vocabulary contexts (as a relatively rare English word for a specific cultural garment)

A yashmak is a traditional veil made of two pieces of thin fabric, worn by some Muslim women to cover the face in public, leaving only the eyes visible — most historically associated with Ottoman Turkey.
